name: Beetroot juice hair dye

card.summary: Beetroot juice is a kitchen colourant people apply to hair for a temporary reddish or auburn tint without chemical dye.
card.note: Colour is temporary and stains skin, fabric and surfaces.

quick.overview:
Beetroot juice contains betanin, the red pigment also used industrially as a food colourant. People mix the juice with a carrier oil or use it as a rinse to give hair a subtle red or auburn cast, as an alternative to boxed dye.

The result is described as mild and short-lived: a dermatologist-authored consumer article says it stains hair with a reddish tint, and a magazine writer reports an auburn glow maintained with weekly rinses. No clinical studies of beetroot as a hair dye were found.
quick.how: Home recipes combine concentrated beet juice with an oil such as olive, argan or coconut, apply it to the hair, cover it and leave it for roughly an hour before rinsing; repeating the process deepens colour. Some users add black tea and wash less often to prolong the tint.
quick.risks: Beetroot juice stains skin, clothing and sinks. Natural dyes are said to fade faster than chemical dyes, and results vary with starting hair colour. No safety data specific to beetroot hair application was found; eating beetroot can turn urine red (beeturia), described as harmless.

lead: Beetroot juice hair dye is a do-it-yourself way to add a temporary red or auburn tint to hair using the pigment in beets. Betanin, a betalain pigment, is used industrially as a red food colouring [1].

People choose it as a kitchen-ingredient alternative to chemical dyes. A dermatologist-written article describes mixing concentrated beet juice with an oil, applying it, covering and leaving it for 60-80 minutes, and repeating to deepen colour [2]. A Bustle writer describes weekly beet rinses, with black tea added to prolong the tint, giving a temporary auburn glow [3].
Beetroot is a much milder colourant than permanent dye, and no clinical research on it as a hair colourant was found.

angle.text: The juice deposits a reddish tint on hair, which users apply to add warmth or auburn tones without chemical dye. The change is subtle and temporary.

paras: Beetroot's red colour comes from betanin, a betacyanin that is used as a red food colourant in sauces, desserts and sweets. The pigment is not broken down in the body, which is why heavy beet intake can colour urine [1].

As a hair product, the juice is used on its own or blended with oil. The article by Akanksha Shah Sanghvi, MD, a clinical dermatologist, says it can stain hair reddish and gives a deeper colour than carrot juice, and that natural dyes may not last as long as chemical ones [2].
The described routine is to mix concentrated juice with an oil, apply, cover the hair and leave it on for an hour or more before rinsing and conditioning. Repeated applications build depth [2].

A Bustle writer who used beets as a gentler alternative to chemical dye reported a temporary auburn tint with weekly rinses, with black tea said to help it last, and noted that beet rinses are easier to remove from sinks than traditional dye [3]. Longevity advice in consumer articles includes limiting heat styling [2].

Henna has been used as a hair dye since antiquity and gives orange to burgundy shades depending on the hair; it is often blended with indigo or cassia. Some products sold as black henna contain para-phenylenediamine, which can cause severe allergic reactions [4]. Beetroot is a food-based option in the same broad family of plant colourants.
